title: Ben Sira and His Book
lead: Jesus son of Sirach, called Ben Sira, was a Jerusalem teacher of wisdom who wrote his book in Hebrew about 180 BC; his grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt in 132 BC (both dates as Rendsburg and Binstein give them). The book, known as Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, is Scripture in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, is among the Apocrypha for Protestants, and is outside the Jewish Bible, though the rabbis quoted it.

sections.b: Near the end of his book the author signs his name: "I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem" (Sirach 50:27). "Son of Sirach" gives the book its Greek name, Sirach, and the man his Hebrew one, Ben Sira. He ran a school, a "house of instruction" (Sirach 51:23), for young men, and his book gathers his teaching on God, wisdom, the law, family, money, speech and friendship. His grandson, who does not give his own name, explains in a Greek prologue that he came to Egypt "in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes," found the book there, and translated it for Jews "living as foreigners in other lands" (Sirach 1:0). The first king called Euergetes reigned only twenty-five years; the second shared the throne from 170 BC and counted his years from then, so his thirty-eighth year is 132 BC (Gigot, Catholic Encyclopedia). The grandson warns that Hebrew does not carry the same force in Greek, and where the Hebrew survives it often differs from his Greek.

For centuries the book was known only in Greek, Latin and Syriac. In 1896 pages of the Hebrew were identified among the manuscripts of the Cairo Genizah, the storeroom of an old synagogue; in the end pages of six medieval manuscripts were found there. Older Hebrew came from Qumran and Masada: a small fragment from Qumran Cave 2 (2Q18) with letters of Sirach 6:14–31, the great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPsa), and a scroll from Masada; these date from about 50 BC to about AD 70. All told, the Hebrew manuscripts give about two-thirds of the book (Rendsburg and Binstein). Where they can be compared with the grandson's Greek they often differ; since most of the Hebrew is in medieval copies, some differences may be the translator's and some later changes in the Hebrew.

sections.h: Echoes in the New Testament and beyond
sections.b: The New Testament never names Ben Sira, but some of its sayings are close to his. James's "let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk, slow to anger" (James 1:19) stands close to Sirach 5:11, and James 5:11 ends with God's pity and mercy as Sirach 2:11 does; Jesus' invitation to take his yoke and find rest (Matthew 11:28–30) follows the pattern of Wisdom's yoke (Sirach 6:24–31; 51:26). Whether these are borrowings or shared Jewish wisdom is debated. The early Christian Didache closely echoes Sirach 4:31 (Didache 4:5). The Babylonian Talmud quotes "the book of Ben Sira" by name (Hagigah 13a, quoting Sirach 3:21–22) and records a debate whether it may be read (Sanhedrin 100b).
